questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Convert polar coordinates to Cartesian form
questions.stem: One study group converts the polar point (r, theta) = (4, pi/3) to Cartesian coordinates. Explain the conversion and give the resulting coordinates.

answer.exemplar: The polar point lies 4 units from the origin along a ray making an angle of pi/3 with the positive horizontal axis. Since the cosine of pi/3 is one half and the sine of pi/3 is the square root of three over two, the Cartesian coordinates are x = 4 times one half = 2 and y = 4 times the square root of three over two = 2 times the square root of three, roughly 3.46. The pair (2, 2 times the square root of three) is therefore the Cartesian location, and squaring and adding the coordinates recovers the radius of 4.

questions.explanation: A polar point gives a distance and a direction, and the Cartesian coordinates are its projections on the two axes, obtained from x = r cos theta and y = r sin theta.
questions.hint: Project the radius onto each axis.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the polar radius is a distance
questions.stem: One study group explains why the polar radius of a Cartesian point is the distance of that point from the origin. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The polar coordinates of a point record a distance and an angle, so the radius r must be the distance from the origin to the point, whatever the point happens to be. In Cartesian terms that distance is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs x and y, so r equals the square root of x squared plus y squared. For the point (3, 4) this gives r = 5, since the triangle is a three-four-five triangle, and the accompanying angle is the one whose tangent is y over x. The two descriptions therefore carry exactly the same information, packaged differently.

questions.explanation: Polar coordinates record a distance and a direction, so r is the distance from the origin to the point, the square root of x squared plus y squared. The angle records the direction.
questions.hint: One is a hypotenuse, the other a direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the curvature of a circle depends on its radius
questions.stem: Another group argues that a circle of radius 4 and a circle of radius 8 bend at the same rate because both are circles. Explain why this is wrong.

answer.exemplar: The curvature of a circle is the reciprocal of its radius, so a circle of radius 4 has curvature 1/4 while a circle of radius 8 has curvature 1/8. Curvature measures how sharply a path bends per unit of length, and the smaller circle achieves the same change of direction over a much shorter distance, so it bends more sharply. The ratio of the two curvatures is 2, in favour of the smaller circle, and this is why a roundabout of small radius forces drivers to reduce speed much more than a wide one of the same angular sweep.

questions.explanation: Curvature is the reciprocal of the radius for a circle, so doubling the radius halves the curvature. The smaller circle changes direction over a shorter distance and therefore bends more sharply.
questions.hint: Halving the radius doubles the curvature.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the arc length of a spiral is set up
questions.stem: Another group explains how the arc length of an Archimedean spiral r = 2 theta is set up over 0 <= theta <= 3. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The polar arc length formula integrates the speed of the point as the parameter advances, and the speed in polar form is the square root of r squared plus r prime squared, with r prime taken with respect to the parameter. Substituting r = 2 theta and r prime = 2 gives an integrand of the square root of 4 theta squared plus 4, which is 2 times the square root of theta squared plus 1. That integrand must then be integrated over the interval from 0 to 3, an antiderivative involving both an algebraic term and a logarithm, so the resulting length has no simple closed form in elementary terms and is usually reported numerically.

questions.explanation: The integrand is the square root of r squared plus r prime squared, with r prime the rate of change of the radius. Substituting the spiral's rule turns the length into one integral over the interval.
questions.hint: Plug the spiral into the polar formula.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the area of a limaçon is obtained
questions.stem: Limaçon area: another group explains how the area enclosed by a limaçon r = a + b sin theta is found. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The region swept by a polar radius is found by integrating one half of the square of the radius over the parameter interval, since a small wedge of angle d theta at radius r has area one half r squared d theta. For the limaçon the radius is a + b sin theta, so the integrand becomes one half of a squared plus 2ab sin theta plus b squared sin squared theta. Over a full revolution the sine term integrates to zero, the constant term contributes pi a squared, and the sine squared term contributes one half of pi b squared, so the total area is pi a squared plus one half of pi b squared, with no cross term surviving.

questions.explanation: A thin polar wedge of radius r and angle d theta has area one half r squared d theta, so the region comes from integrating that. Over a full turn the cross term vanishes.
questions.hint: Integrate one half of r squared.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain the origin of the polar arc length integrand
questions.stem: Integrand derivation: another group explains how the polar arc length integrand is obtained from the motion of the point. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: As the parameter advances by a small amount d theta, the point moves along the radius by dr and sideways by r d theta, so the two displacements are perpendicular and combine in quadrature. The total small length is therefore the square root of dr squared plus r squared d theta squared, which after dividing by d theta becomes the square root of r prime squared plus r squared. Integrating that speed against d theta over the parameter interval gives the arc length of the curve, and the same reasoning explains why the integrand depends on both the radius and its rate of change.

questions.explanation: A small parameter step moves the point radially by dr and sideways by r d theta, and those perpendicular displacements combine in quadrature. Dividing by d theta gives the speed to be integrated.
questions.hint: Radial and sideways parts.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the area of a rose curve is obtained
questions.stem: Rose area derivation: another group explains how the area of a rose curve is obtained from the polar area formula. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The area of a polar region is one half of the integral of the square of the radius over the parameter interval, because a thin wedge of angle d theta at radius r has area one half r squared d theta. For the rose r = a cos of n theta the squared radius becomes a squared cos squared of n theta, and the cosine squared term averages to one half over each period, which turns the integral into a simple multiple of pi. For even n the rose is traced twice over a full revolution and the total area works out as pi a squared over 2, while for odd n it is traced once over 0 to pi and the total area is pi a squared over 4. Each petal therefore encloses the same share of the total, since the petals are congruent.

questions.explanation: A thin polar wedge has area one half r squared d theta, so integrating that gives the region. The cosine squared term averages to one half per period, so the area is a multiple of pi a squared.
questions.hint: Wedge areas, then average the cosine.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the curvature of a circle scales with its radius
questions.stem: Another group explains what happens to the curvature of a circle when its radius is tripled. Give the explanation.

answer.exemplar: The curvature of a circle is the reciprocal of its radius, so tripling the radius divides the curvature by three. A circle of radius 3 has curvature 1/3, and the same circle stretched to radius 9 has curvature 1/9. The reason is that curvature measures how sharply the direction of travel changes per unit of distance, and the wider circle has to turn through exactly the same total angle spread over three times as much road. The turning itself is unchanged; what changes is the rate at which it happens relative to the distance covered.

questions.explanation: Curvature is the reciprocal of the radius, so tripling the radius divides the curvature by three. The same turn is spread over three times the distance, so the change of direction is a third as large.
questions.hint: Curvature falls in inverse proportion.
